newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada vows to set own salmon fishing quotas.
newsitem.headline: Canada vows to set own salmon fishing quotas.

text.p: Canada has given up trying to reach a deal with the United States over salmon fishing on the West Coast, Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Thursday.
Instead, Canada will put an end to months of turbulent talks and set its own salmon quotas.
"We will be proceeding to introduce our own fishing requirements," Axworthy told a news conference in Ottawa.
"I regret very much that we weren't able to find a deal with the Americans. There isn't a technique that we haven't used to find a resolution in this matter."
Fisheries Minister David Anderson will make the details of Canada's fishing quota public soon.
The U.S. State Department acknowledged in Washington that attempts to resolve the dispute failed, despite hopes by both sides of reaching a settlement before the start of the salmon fishing season.

"In the absence of an agreement this summer, U.S. managers will ensure that our 1997 fisheries are conducted in accordance with sound conservation and management principles and will coordinate with Canadian managers to that end," the State Department said.
Canada and the United States have held sporadic talks over the past few months on how to divide the Pacfic salmon catch.
Talks initially broke down in May after Canada accused the United States of bargaining in bad faith.
The governments of Canada and the province of British Columbia threatened reprisals to pressure the United States into establishing fishing quotas.

Canada announced last month it would begin enforcing requirements that U.S. boats fishing in Canadian waters report to Canadian authorities. Under that policy, the Canadian Coast Guard seized four U.S. fishing boats.
Washington blamed Canada for the breakdown in talks, saying Ottawa had been unwilling to make efforts to conserve coho salmon stocks off the West Coast.

"In the end, Canada wanted the United States to make a substantial reduction in its sockeye fishery in return for a coho regime that would not ensure conservation and would not provide a coho fishery for the United States," the State Department said.
Axworthy, made clear on Thursday he believed the only remaining course would be for the dispute to be settled through binding arbitration.
The United States has turned down previous Canadian requests for arbitration.
The dispute went to non-binding arbitration in 1995, but collapsed without a deal.
Axworthy said the two countries were closer to a deal now than then and he rejected the use of reprisals to force the Americans' hand.
"We should be very careful not to extend linkages in this issue," he said. "This is a fishing issue...it's very important that we resolve it within those parameters."
